title: Deixis and anaphora
description: Explore how utterances anchor reference to speaker, place and time, and how anaphors, pronouns, pro-forms and reduced clauses depend on antecedents.
example: She left her keys here yesterday, but now they are over there.

Anaphora in which the anaphor precedes its antecedent.
A reduced expression that stands for a larger expression or clause.

A form such as each other or one another expressing a mutual relation.
A determinative or pronoun such as this or that used for deixis or anaphora.

intro: Stand in a cluttered room and say *Put this with those boxes over there*. Every italicised word asks the listener to look outward: *this* and *those* divide the space by distance from the speaker, while *there* points beyond immediate reach. Quote the same sentence in an email and the instructions lose their targets. That dependence on who is speaking, where and when is deixis. A pronoun such as *they* can instead send the listener back to an earlier phrase, and that backward dependence is anaphora. The two relations often meet in a single form.

The chapter begins with that contrast, then follows it through personal pronouns, reflexives, reciprocals and demonstratives. Reduced noun phrases and verb phrases come next, including *one*, *do so* and *so*, together with ellipsis and gapping. The closing sections turn to spatial and temporal deixis, and to what happens when the deictic centre shifts from speaker to addressee or to a reported participant.

The question to keep asking is where an interpretation comes from: from the utterance situation, from an earlier expression, or from material omitted but recoverable. The interesting cases draw on more than one source.

blocks.text: *Could you pick this up and put it with those boxes?* The request works only if you know who is being addressed, which object *this* picks out, and which boxes *those* marks as relatively distant. Person, place and time all enter the interpretation. When reference depends on such features of the utterance-act, the expression is deictic.

Deictic expressions change referent from utterance to utterance, but they do so systematically: the first person pronoun belongs to whoever is speaking, a place adverb such as *here* names a region containing the speaker, and *yesterday* picks out the day before the utterance. *I bought a new stereo yesterday* shows person and time working together in one short sentence. A proper name can vary in reference too, yet its meaning does not build in that relation to the utterance-act.

A deictic expression may contain a smaller deictic marker. The whole noun phrase *those boxes* is the expression, while *those* carries the meaning ‘relatively distant from the speaker’. *Last week* splits the same way: the phrase locates a span, and *last* supplies the orientation.

check.prompt: Why is here deictic but Paris is not?

options.text: Here is interpreted relative to the place of utterance; Paris has a place-based meaning independent of the utterance.
options.feedback: Deictic meaning is systematically tied to the utterance-act.

options.text: Paris is a proper name and proper names are never deictic.
options.feedback: A proper name can be used deictically in some contexts, but its meaning is not inherently utterance-anchored.
Here is a locative expression, not a preposition.

blocks.text: *Max claims he wasn’t told.* Who is *he*? The natural answer is Max, and that answer comes not from the situation but from an earlier expression in the same sentence. The pronoun is an anaphor, *Max* its antecedent, and the relation between them is anaphora.

The antecedent need not sit in the same clause, or even the same sentence. In *I’ve just been talking to Max. I understand that Ed has told Frank that the report has exonerated him*, the pronoun could point to Max, Ed or Frank. Grammar leaves the options open; context, emphasis and careful writing close them down. A reader who has to stop and ask who *him* is has met the cost of an unresolved chain.

Order matters. Put the pronoun after its antecedent — *When the headmaster saw the damage, he called the police* — and resolution is immediate. Put it first, as in *When he saw the damage, the headmaster called the police*, and the listener must hold a pronoun in mind until the noun arrives. The second pattern, anticipatory anaphora, is possible but more restricted.

sections.title: Personal pronouns: first and second person

blocks.text: Say *I’ll be there* and *I* picks out whoever is speaking; say *You left it there* and *you* picks out the addressee. These are the primary uses of the first and second person. The first person covers *I*, *me*, *my*, *mine*, *myself* and the plurals *we*, *us*, *our*, *ours*, *ourselves*; the second covers *you*, *your*, *yours*, *yourself* and *yourselves*. Everything else falls into the third person, the unmarked category.

Both persons stretch beyond their primary use. An authorial *we* may include the writer and exclude the reader, or invite the reader in; *We’re going to be late* can do either. *You* can mean people in general, as in *You can’t tell these days*. The examples below keep those secondary uses visible.

*She said, ‘I am tired’* keeps *I* with the original speaker; *She said she was tired* shifts the pronoun to the reporter’s perspective. Because first and second person are anchored to the utterance, they move when speech is reported. The deictic centre is not always the current speaker, and free indirect style exploits exactly that instability.

items.note: I refers to the speaker.
Generic you: people in general.
We may include or exclude the addressee.

blocks.text: *They say it will rain.* Who are they? No identifiable group need be involved. The pronoun is neither pointing to a situation nor picking up an antecedent; it is generic. Third person is the default category, and it can also be anaphoric, as in *Max left because he was tired*, or deictic, as in *He’s the one over there*. The form alone does not settle the relation.

*Max thinks he is clever* normally has *he* mean Max; *Max thinks his brother is clever* does not. Where an antecedent is available, the semantic link can be identity, inclusion or exclusion. *His* can include Max in the possessive relation, but the person said to be clever is the brother. Number and gender narrow the search, yet neither determines it.

*When he saw the damage, the headmaster called the police* is acceptable; pushing the pronoun deeper into embedded structure makes the sentence harder to process. Anticipatory anaphora is permitted under narrower conditions, especially when the pronoun sits in a subordinate clause and its antecedent in the matrix. Syntax, discourse structure and the type of pronoun all bear on the result.

items.text: Max left because he was tired.
items.note: Anaphoric he refers to Max.
Deictic he refers to a person in the situation.

They is deictic to people in the situation.

blocks.text: English prefers to name a referent before pronominalising it. *When the headmaster saw the damage, he called the police* runs with that preference: the noun phrase arrives first, and *he* collects it. Reverse the two, as in *When he saw the damage, the headmaster called the police*, and the sentence still works, but the listener must wait for the noun to settle who *he* is.

*When he saw the damage, the headmaster called the police* is easy enough; bury the pronoun deeper and the sentence becomes harder to process. The reversed order is not free. Anticipatory anaphora is easiest when the pronoun is in a subordinate clause and the antecedent in the matrix. The type of antecedent matters too: a definite noun phrase in a prominent position is easier to anticipate than an indefinite one buried in a modifier.

Processing pressure explains part of the pattern. A retrospective pronoun resolves against material already heard; an anticipatory one creates a temporary gap that the rest of the sentence must fill. Writers exploit it when syntax narrows the possibilities sharply enough to make the delay safe.

items.text: When the headmaster saw the damage, he called the police.
items.note: Retrospective: he follows the headmaster.

items.text: When he saw the damage, the headmaster called the police.
items.note: Anticipatory: he precedes the headmaster.

blocks.text: *It’s raining.* What is *it*? Nothing in the situation answers the question, and no earlier phrase supplies a referent. Weather *it* is a subject without an entity behind it. The same form does refer in *I found the key and put it in my pocket*, where it picks up *the key*, and it can name an abstract situation in *It was a mistake*.

*It is clear that he’s guilty* gives *it* no referent of its own. The clause *that he’s guilty* is the extraposed subject, and *it* merely holds the subject slot until the clause arrives. Clefts use the same pronoun for a different job: *It was Kim who called* foregrounds Kim by splitting one proposition into two parts.
Anaphoric *it* needs an antecedent; weather *it* does not; dummy *it* has no referent at all and exists because the clause requires a subject. These uses are not interchangeable.

items.note: Anaphoric it refers to the key.

blocks.text: *She hurt herself* and *She hurt her* differ by more than emphasis. The reflexive points back to the subject of its own clause; the ordinary pronoun points elsewhere. English uses *myself*, *yourself*, *himself*, *herself*, *itself*, *ourselves*, *yourselves* and *themselves* for this local anaphora, typically in complement function.

The antecedent normally sits in the same local domain, often the same clause. *She hurt herself* satisfies that condition; *She said that I hurt herself* does not, because *herself* would need an antecedent within the embedded clause, and *I* cannot supply it. Noun phrases and dual-head constructions can be domains too, so proximity on the page does not decide the boundary.

Some reflexives appear where a plain pronoun would be expected. *They elected the president himself* and *The manager spoke to Kim and myself* add emphasis or mark a particular point of view; these are override reflexives. Emphatic reflexives form a related but distinct pattern, as in *She herself wrote the letter*, where the reflexive reinforces a noun phrase rather than filling a complement.

Reflexive complement with plural antecedent.

blocks.text: *She hurt herself* is grammatical because the reflexive and its antecedent share a clause. *She said that I hurt herself* fails because *herself* looks for an antecedent inside the embedded clause, and the only candidate there is *I*. Binding is easiest to see in that contrast.

*The teacher spoke to the student about herself* can point to the teacher or the student, depending on context and structure. The antecedent is often the subject of the local domain, but not always. Syntax constrains the search without always producing one answer.

Override reflexives sit outside the basic pattern. They occur where a non-reflexive pronoun would be expected, as in *They elected the president himself* or *The manager spoke to Kim and myself*, and they usually add emphasis or signal a point of view. Emphatic reflexives such as *She herself wrote the letter* are a separate use, related by form rather than by complement structure.

blocks.text: *They helped each other* describes a relation running in both directions: each member of the group helped and was helped. *Each other* and *one another* are the reciprocal pronouns, and both require a plural or group antecedent. The relation holds among members of that group, not between one antecedent and one anaphor.
Reciprocals occupy many of the positions reflexives do: object (*They distrust each other*), prepositional complement (*They spoke to each other*), and genitive (*They read each other’s work*).

*They followed each other* can describe a line in which each person follows the one ahead, not a pair who follow one another simultaneously. Mutuality is not always symmetrical. The predicate and the context decide whether the relation is pairwise, collective or sequential, which is why reciprocal meaning cannot be read off the pronoun alone.

blocks.text: Put two bowls on a table and say *This bowl holds more than that one*. The demonstratives divide the space around the speaker: *this* is relatively close, *that* relatively distant. The same forms also point backward in discourse. *He wants $30, but that’s too much* uses *that* for the price just mentioned, not for an object in the room.

*This report* uses a demonstrative as a determiner; *This is important* uses one as a pronoun. *These* and *those* agree with plural nouns, and the deictic meaning can be spatial, temporal or discourse-based.

Even anaphoric demonstratives keep a trace of that spatial meaning. *That* can suggest distance from the speaker’s current focus; *this* can suggest closeness. Grammar does not dictate the choice. It tells the reader how the speaker is positioning the referent, and that positioning is part of the meaning.

sections.title: Pro-nominal one, other, and fused heads

blocks.text: *I need a pen; do you have one?* The second *one* does not introduce a new pen; it stands for the kind of thing already mentioned. This is the pro-nominal use of *one*, an anaphoric device that often appears in fused-head constructions such as *the red one* or *a good one*. *One* can also be a numeral or a generic pronoun, so the construction has to be identified before the meaning is fixed.

*Other* has a similar double life. In *I’ll take this one and you take the other*, it is pro-nominal and depends on an antecedent set; in *Other people disagreed*, it is a determinative modifying a noun. The pro-nominal use typically contrasts one member or subset with another.

*The rich* packs two functions into one form; *I’ll take the red one* leaves a gap for context to fill. Fused heads and ellipsis are related but not identical. In a fused head, one expression performs the head function together with a dependent function. In ellipsis, material is left out but recovered.

blocks.text: A stranded auxiliary can carry a whole predicate. Ask *Can you finish by Friday?* and the answer *I could* means *I could finish by Friday*. The auxiliary remains, the rest of the verb phrase disappears, and the context supplies what is missing. *She has* and *They won’t* work the same way.

*She left and I did so too* lets *did so* carry the earlier verb phrase. *Do it* and *do that* contain a pronoun object and usually point to a specific action, as in *I’ll do it tomorrow*. The forms look similar, but they differ in what they can replace and in how specific their reference is.

*I think so*, *I hope so* and *They said so* use *so* as a pro-form for a clause or proposition. It has other lives too: deictic in *Hold it just so*, connective in *So we left*. Only the construction tells you which *so* you are dealing with.

items.note: Auxiliary stranding for a full predicate.

items.text: She left and I did so too.
items.note: Do so replaces the verb phrase.
Do it with a specific action pronoun.

blocks.text: *Hope you’re well* drops *I* and the auxiliary from the start of a main clause. An open interrogative can shrink to *Why?*, a declarative response to *Me too*, and a coordination to *Kim likes tea and Pat coffee*. In each case the missing material is recoverable from context.

*Kim likes tea and Pat coffee* is understood as *Kim likes tea and Pat likes coffee*: the verb is absent from the second conjunct, while its subject and object remain. Gapping is the coordination case. Listeners restore the verb from the structure of the coordination.

A pro-form supplies an overt replacement; ellipsis leaves a gap. Ellipsis is not the same as a pro-form. The two can combine when an auxiliary is stranded and the rest of the predicate is ellipted, as in *I could*.

sections.title: Spatial deixis: here, there, come and go

blocks.text: *I was born in London and have lived here all my life.* The *here* refers to London, but not because *here* means London. It means a place containing the speaker at the time of speaking, and the antecedent supplies London as the value. The expression is deictic in its meaning and anaphoric in its resolution.

*Come* and *go* carry a similar orientation. *Come here* describes movement towards the speaker or addressee; *Go there* describes movement away. Which end counts as the centre depends on who is speaking and who is being addressed, so the same verb can reverse direction when the perspective changes.

Spatial expressions can also take their source from the discourse. *She lived too far away* means away from the speaker, or away from a place already mentioned; the context decides. The expression keeps its relational meaning even when the reference point is recovered anaphorically.

items.note: Here includes the speaker’s location.
There is relatively distant from the speaker.
Come describes movement towards the speaker.
Away is interpreted relative to a contextually supplied source.

sections.title: Temporal deixis and shift of centre

blocks.text: *I’ll do it now* places the action at a time that includes the utterance. *Now* and *then* are the basic temporal deictics — *then* pointing to a time relatively distant or supplied by the discourse — and they are joined by *today*, *yesterday*, *tomorrow*, *last week* and *ago*, all of which locate a time relative to the moment of speaking.

Temporal expressions can also be anaphoric. *She was stunned, but soon recovered* interprets *soon* relative to the being stunned, not to the utterance. *He left at least a week ago* may be measured from the utterance or from a reported perspective.

The deictic centre can shift. A public notice reading *Now wash your hands* means the time of reading, not the time of writing; reported speech can locate temporal expressions at the reported participant’s viewpoint. Once the centre moves, every deictic in the sentence may move with it.

items.note: Now includes the utterance time.

items.note: Soon is interpreted relative to being stunned.

blocks.text: *She is taller than her brother* contains more than it appears to. The comparative clause *than her brother* is reduced: it is understood as *than her brother is tall*, with the adjective and its degree recovered from the matrix. The single noun phrase stands in for a whole clause, and the missing material is supplied by the matrix rather than guessed from context.

Reduction can leave only a single element. *Bob is as generous as Sue* keeps just the second term, and *She is taller than him* does the same. Case forms vary: formal writing may prefer *than I*, informal speech usually has *than me*, and both are interpreted through the reduced clause.

Not every comparative clause can be filled out. *She wrote more plays than he wrote five novels* fails because the measure corresponding to *more* must stay empty in the comparative clause; the clause is structurally reduced, not a full clause with a numeral added.

items.note: Understood as than her brother is tall.

blocks.text: *Two letters arrived for Jill; she will pick them up.* The pronoun *she* reaches back to Jill, and *them* to the letters. Reference here is not confined to one sentence: it is a thread running through the discourse, and the reader follows it by keeping track of what has already been introduced.

*She* and *them* are enough once Jill and the letters are established. Discourse-old information is easy to pronominalise. Discourse-new information usually needs a fuller noun phrase, especially when it is the focus of the sentence. A writer who pronominalises too early leaves the reader searching for an antecedent that has not yet arrived.

Ambiguity appears when several antecedents remain available. *I’ve just been talking to Max. I understand that Ed has told Frank that the report has exonerated him* allows Max, Ed or Frank. Grammar permits all three; context may favour one.

Topic and focus shape the choice as well. A pronoun is easiest to resolve when its antecedent is the current topic or a salient participant. A change of topic often calls for a full noun phrase, and a long-distance pronoun can stay ambiguous even when syntax permits only one structural antecedent.

blocks.text: A pronoun can look outward to the situation or backward to a phrase, and the difference between those directions organises the chapter. Deixis anchors reference to the utterance-act: person, place and time. A deictic expression may contain a smaller marker, an indexing act may help identify the referent, and the deictic centre normally sits with the speaker — though it can move to the addressee or a reported participant.

The relation is retrospective when the anaphor follows its antecedent, anticipatory when it precedes it. Anaphora can also coexist with deixis, as *here* does when it means the place just named. Personal pronouns, reflexives, reciprocals and demonstratives each bring their own patterns of local and long-distance dependence.

Reduced noun phrases and verb phrases rely on pro-forms and ellipsis. *One*, *other*, *do so*, *do it* and *so* stand in for larger expressions; ellipsis omits recoverable material, including the gapped verb of a coordination. Spatial and temporal deixis complete the system, with *here* and *there*, *come* and *go*, *now* and *then*, and the shifts of centre that keep the apparatus flexible.

blocks.title: A reference checklist
blocks.text: Ask where the interpretation comes from: the utterance situation (deixis), an antecedent (anaphora), or omitted recoverable material (ellipsis). Identify the deictic centre and any indexing act. For anaphora, locate the antecedent and decide whether the relation is retrospective or anticipatory.

check.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes deixis from anaphora?

options.text: Deixis is anchored to the utterance-act; anaphora is anchored to an antecedent.
options.feedback: The two can overlap, but their sources of interpretation differ.

options.text: Deixis always involves pronouns; anaphora never does.
options.feedback: Both can involve pronouns.
Anticipatory anaphora is also possible.

worked: Take *She left her keys here yesterday, but now they are over there*. *She* and *her* are anaphoric to a contextually salient person; *here* and *there* are locative deictics; *yesterday* and *now* are temporal deictics. *They* is anaphoric to *her keys*.

The example shows deixis and anaphora interacting. *Here* is deictic because it is anchored to the speaker’s location, and it may also be anaphoric if the discourse has established a place. *Now* contrasts with *yesterday* deictically, while *they* depends on the antecedent *her keys*. The interpretation requires both the utterance situation and the discourse context.
application: For each referring expression, ask where its interpretation comes from. If it depends on the speaker, addressee, time or place of utterance, it is deictic. If it depends on an antecedent, it is anaphoric. If it depends on omitted recoverable material, it is elliptical or a pro-form.

Identify the deictic centre and any shift. In ordinary conversation it is the speaker; in a notice it may be the reader; in reported speech it may be a reported participant. Check for indexing acts such as gestures or written arrows.

For anaphora, locate the antecedent and decide whether the relation is retrospective or anticipatory. For reflexives and reciprocals, check the local domain and the type of relation. For reduced VPs, identify what the pro-form or ellipsis stands for.
reveal: In *She left her keys here yesterday, but now they are over there*, *here* and *there* are locative deictics, *yesterday* and *now* are temporal deictics, *she/her* are anaphoric to a salient person, and *they* is anaphoric to *her keys*. The deictic centre is the speaker’s current situation.
recap: Deixis anchors reference to the utterance-act; anaphora anchors it to an antecedent. Deictic expressions can contain deictic markers, and indexing acts can clarify reference. The deictic centre is usually the speaker but can shift.

Pronouns, reflexives, reciprocals and demonstratives have distinct anaphoric and deictic uses. Pro-forms and ellipsis reduce NPs and VPs, and spatial and temporal deixis organise location and time around the utterance.

self_check.question: What is deixis?
self_check.answer: Reference determined by features of the utterance-act, such as speaker, addressee, time and place.

self_check.question: What is the difference between anaphora and deixis?
self_check.answer: Anaphora is interpretation through an antecedent; deixis is interpretation through the utterance situation.

self_check.question: What is anticipatory anaphora?
self_check.answer: Anaphora in which the anaphor precedes its antecedent, as in When he saw the damage, the headmaster called the police.

self_check.question: What is the difference between a basic and an emphatic reflexive?
self_check.answer: A basic reflexive fills a complement role; an emphatic reflexive adds emphasis.

self_check.question: What is gapping?
self_check.answer: Ellipsis of a repeated verb in a coordination, as in Kim likes tea and Pat coffee.
